passage: When a student march against a fee hike was announced, four teens made up their minds in very different ways. Madhav read the notice, then the college's statement, then three news reports written by different papers. He looked into who was organising it and what exactly they were demanding. Eshaan sat quietly and asked which value counted most to him, be it safety or fairness, and if walking in the march would really serve it. A letter, a petition or a word at the school council might do more, he thought. Gargi went because her friends were going. She felt the buzz and the fear of being left out, and she never learned what the demands were. When voices rose near the gate, she had no idea what she was standing for or how to slip away. Kabir had planned to go too, but the morning's reports said the gathering had turned tense. He stayed home and helped make posters for a peaceful awareness stall at school instead.

qa.q: What did Madhav read before deciding about the march?
qa.a: He read the notice, the college's statement and three news reports.

qa.q: How does Gargi's reason for going differ from Eshaan's reasoning, and what followed?
qa.a: Gargi went because friends were going and did not know the demands, so she was lost when voices rose. Eshaan asked which principle mattered most and whether marching served it, and considered a letter or council meeting.

qa.q: What might Gargi be feeling when voices rise near the gate?
qa.a: She is probably anxious and uncertain, since she does not know what she stands for or how to leave.

qa.q: What could Gargi do the next time friends invite her to a protest?
qa.a: She could ask what it is about and who is organising it, and agree with a trusted adult how she would leave if things get tense. 🙂

grounding: Four teens decide about a student protest by gathering facts, reasoning from values, following friends, and changing plan when the news shifts.

passage: After a post of hers was badly received, Sonali opened her phone to hundreds of hostile comments. Her hands shook, but she put the phone down and decided to wait a day. By morning the heat inside her had cooled, and she was glad she had not typed anything at midnight. Omkar took a different first step. He made his accounts private, muted certain words, saved screenshots of the threatening messages and reported them to the platform. He did all that before saying anything in public. Santosh answered comment after comment through the night. Each reply pulled in new attacks and fresh screenshots, and by dawn he was worn out and shaking. Weeks later, Sonali returned with a smaller circle of followers. She looked at messages just at chosen hours and saw a counsellor to talk through the strain, slowly building a calmer bond with the site.

qa.q: What did Omkar save before saying anything in public?
qa.a: He saved screenshots of the threatening messages.

qa.q: How does Santosh's response to the comments differ from Sonali's, and what happened to each?
qa.a: Santosh replied all night, which drew fresh attacks and left him exhausted. Sonali waited a day, so her emotion dropped and she did not add fuel.

qa.q: What was Santosh probably feeling as he answered comment after comment?
qa.a: He was likely angry and desperate to set things straight, though it left him worn out and shaking.

qa.q: What could Santosh do now?
qa.a: He could stop replying, lock his accounts, save the abusive messages and report them, then talk to someone he trusts or a counsellor. 🤍

grounding: Four students respond to an online pile-on by pausing, protecting accounts and saving evidence, replying to everyone, and returning with limits and support.

passage: Four students were thinking about careers, and they went about it in different ways. Sabina asked herself what a good career ought to feel like day to day before naming a single job. She wanted independence, a dependable pay cheque and a job that helps people, and only then checked which fields matched. Arjun scored medicine, engineering and design for interest, effort, cost and job security, gave each a weight, and saw that his favourite depended heavily on how much he had weighted salary. Rohan chose the science stream because both his father and his older brother are engineers. He never asked whether he liked it, and by Class 11 he was restless and concealing bad marks. Farida scored poorly in chemistry even with steady effort. She met the school counsellor, admitted that medicine might not suit her, and moved towards the route through data and statistics she had kept away from.

qa.q: What did Sabina want from a working life?
qa.a: She wanted independence, a dependable pay cheque and a job that helps people.

qa.q: How does Rohan's choice differ from Farida's, and what happened to each?
qa.a: Rohan followed his father and brother without asking whether he liked it, and ended up bored and hiding marks. Farida saw her chemistry results, met the counsellor and shifted to a path that fit.

qa.q: What might Rohan be feeling as he hides his poor marks?
qa.a: He is probably worried and ashamed, since he did not choose the stream for himself and fears letting the family down.

qa.q: What could Rohan do now?
qa.a: He could tell his family honestly how he feels and ask a school counsellor about options that match his interests. 🙂

grounding: Four students choose a career by asking what a good working life should feel like, scoring options, following family expectation, and revisiting after weak results.

passage: Four project leads each had to settle a clash among teams, and each went about it differently. Tanvir drew a map of everyone affected: sales wanted speed, engineers wanted quality, and finance wanted low cost. Beside each group he wrote down what it really worried about, not only what it demanded. Payal chose no side. She asked what would satisfy every key need, and proposed launching a limited set of features now, with the quality work coming in the next release. Ojas gave in to whoever pushed hardest each time, and his quieter teams felt ignored. The product drifted as decisions followed pressure instead of the larger aim. Meera announced her decision and then went to see the team that had lost. She explained her reasons and agreed a follow-up on their concerns, so the relationship stayed sound for later decisions.

qa.q: What did Tanvir write beside each group?
qa.a: He wrote what each group really worried about, not just what it demanded.

qa.q: How does Ojas's way of deciding differ from Payal's, and what happened to the teams?
qa.a: Ojas gave in to the loudest person, so quieter teams felt ignored and the product drifted. Payal asked what would meet every key need and proposed a limited launch now with quality work later.

qa.q: What might the quieter teams be feeling under Ojas?
qa.a: They probably feel ignored and unimportant, since decisions follow whoever presses hardest.

qa.q: What could Ojas do to make decisions fairer?
qa.a: He could ask each team what it truly needs, weigh those needs against the overall goal, and explain the choice to those who lose. 🙂

grounding: Four leads settle conflicting stakeholders by mapping interests, seeking a win-win, giving in to the loudest, and explaining the outcome to the losers.

passage: At the community pool, four children were learning to swim in different ways. Francis was afraid of water, so he began in the shallow end, standing and splashing. If he could feel safe there, he told himself, floating would be the next step. Sameer watched an older swimmer's arms and copied the movement on the poolside. Once in the pool, under the coach's eye, he tried it, and the coach corrected the position of his elbow. Neel wanted to impress his friends and jumped into the deep end when the coach was not looking. He panicked and had to be pulled out by the lifeguard, who wrapped a towel around him. The coach sat down with him, and Neel understood that being brave is not the same as being able. Pooja sank every time she tried to float. The coach noticed that she was stiff. She took a slow breath, loosened her arms and let the water hold her up.

qa.q: Where did Francis start his practice?
qa.a: Francis started by standing in the shallow end and splashing.

qa.q: How does Neel's choice differ from Sameer's, and what happened to each?
qa.a: Neel jumped into the deep end to impress friends and had to be pulled out, while Sameer copied a swimmer's arms and had the coach correct his elbow.

qa.q: What was Neel probably feeling when he was pulled out of the water?
qa.a: He was frightened and shaken; the panic in the water showed him he was not ready.

qa.q: What could Neel do next to build his skill safely?
qa.a: He could practise in the shallow end with the coach and move deeper only when the coach says so. 🙂

grounding: Four children learn to swim by starting in the shallows, copying strokes, jumping in the deep end to seem brave, and relaxing the body to float.

passage: Four teams each faced a product that was not working. Minakshi's team watched new users drift away inside seven days. They asked why five times, and each answer went a step deeper, from a poor first-use flow to finding out that the people using the app were never the ones paying or making the choice. Indu, a founder, phoned fifteen users who had stopped using her fitness app and asked what they did now. Most said they now belonged to a chat group run by a trainer, which pointed to another kind of product. Following two years of effort, Sonali's team kept adding features to one product since stopping felt like admitting the years were wasted. Each release cost more and brought no growth. Kabir and his partners ran six weeks of tests and found no demand. They wound down, refunded advance payments, thanked their users and shared notes on the code, keeping their name good for the next venture.

qa.q: How many lapsed users did Indu phone?
qa.a: Indu phoned fifteen users.

qa.q: How does Sonali's team's choice differ from Kabir's, and what happened to each?
qa.a: Sonali's team kept adding features because stopping felt like a waste, and costs rose with no growth. Kabir and his partners saw no demand after six weeks and wound down cleanly.

qa.q: What might Sonali's team be feeling about stopping?
qa.a: They probably feel attached and afraid of wasting two years, which makes them keep going.

qa.q: What could Sonali's team do to test whether to continue?
qa.a: They could talk to lapsed users like Indu did, set a clear date to check for growth, and decide from what they learn rather than from the years spent. 🙂

grounding: Four teams handle a failing product by tracing the cause, interviewing lapsed users, persisting because of sunk cost, and shutting down cleanly.
